passage:
Okay, so, I'm Nilesh, and the interviewer asked me, "What was the worst part?" Honestly, it wasn't the rumour itself. It was the three weeks of waiting. Somebody in the pantry said, "Cuts are coming to our division," and after that I did the rent maths every night. My EMI, my parents' expectation, my sister's fees. Tarun, my flatmate, found me at the table at 1 am with a calculator.

I could have panicked. I nearly typed an angry post about management. Instead I did the boring things. I moved a little from each salary into a separate account. I updated my resume on a Sunday and quietly messaged two old colleagues. And I kept doing my work well, because I still had it.

Tarun said, "You look like you're planning, not drowning." Some days I was doing both, I'll admit. But planning helped. 🙂

qa.q: What did Nilesh say was the worst part of the layoff rumour?
qa.a: Nilesh said the worst part was the three weeks of waiting after someone in the pantry said cuts were coming.

qa.q: What was Nilesh worried about at the table at 1 am?
qa.a: Nilesh was worried about rent, the EMI, family expectations and a sister's fees, and was doing the maths with a calculator.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do instead of panicking?
qa.a: Nilesh set aside a small buffer each month, updated the resume, quietly messaged two old colleagues and kept doing good work.

qa.q: How does Tarun see Nilesh's state during this time?
qa.a: Tarun sees someone who looks like a planner rather than someone drowning, though Nilesh admits to sometimes doing both at once.

grounding: Nilesh fears rumoured layoffs because of rent, EMIs and family, and responds by building a buffer, updating the resume and continuing to work.
